title: Look Up Keys in a Search Tree

concept.title: Each comparison throws away half of the tree
body: A **binary search tree** (BST) keeps its values in order. In a binary search tree the values are different, and every value in the left subtree of a node is smaller than the node, and every value in the right subtree is larger. To look for a key, compare it with the root: if it is equal, you found it; if it is smaller, the key can only be in the left subtree; if it is larger, only in the right subtree. Each step discards a whole subtree.

In a balanced tree this takes about log2(n) steps; in the worst case (a path) it takes n steps. A loop is enough here, no recursion is needed. Compare with the ordinary binary tree, where a missing value forces you to look at **every** node.

statement: A binary search tree and `q` keys are given. For each key print `yes` if some node of the tree has this value and `no` otherwise, one answer per line.
inputFormat: The first line has `t`, the number of words in the description of the tree.
The second line has the tree in level order: the root first, then the children of the nodes row by row from left to right. `N` stands for a missing child. There is no `N` at the end.
The fourth line has the `q` keys.
constraints: The height of the tree is at most 800.
The tree is a binary search tree (all values are different).

examples.note: The values 3 and 9 are in the tree, 5 is not.

hints: Compare the key with the value of the current node.
If the key is smaller, go to the left child; if it is larger, go to the right child.
If you reach an empty place, the key is not in the tree.
